Back to [Module 1](../lessons/01-rules.qmd).

## Exercise 1.1: Write a rule {#ex-1.1}

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule flagstat:
    input:
        "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_aligned.bam",       # <1>
    output:
        "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_aligned_flagstat.txt",
    shell:
        "samtools flagstat {input} > {output}"                  # <2>
```

1. The input is the output of `align`, spelled exactly the same. That is the
   only link between the two rules: Snakemake matches the strings.
2. `samtools flagstat` prints its report to stdout, so the shell redirects it
   into the declared output.

```bash
snakemake -n -p flagstat
snakemake --cores 1 flagstat
head -1 output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_aligned_flagstat.txt
```

```text
28634 + 0 in total (QC-passed reads + QC-failed reads)
```

28,634 reads, and the report says 28,632 of them mapped (99.99%). That high a
rate is a property of the course data, not of bowtie2: the course FASTQs were
made from reads ENCODE had already placed in the 5 Mb window.

If `align` had not run yet, the dry run would plan two jobs (`align`, then
`flagstat`), plus the index if that were missing too. You asked for one file
and Snakemake found the rest.

## Exercise 1.2: What reruns? {#ex-1.2}

1. Touching the aligned BAM plans nothing.

   ```text
   Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).
   ```

   A touched file is newer than before, but that only matters to jobs that
   *read* it. `align` wrote it, so `align` is still up to date (its inputs
   are older than its output). `fastqc` does not read it. If you had done
   Exercise 1.1, `flagstat` would now be out of date (its input is newer than
   its output), and `snakemake -n flagstat` would plan it.

2. Touching the FASTQ plans both `align` and `fastqc`, one job each, with the
   same reason:

   ```text
       reason: Updated input files: ../../data/fastq/HCT116_CTCF_1.fastq.gz
   ```

   Both rules read that file. `bowtie2_index` does not, so it is not planned.

3. Deleting `output/reference/` and running `snakemake -n` with no target
   plans one job, `bowtie2_index`. With no target, Snakemake makes only the first
   rule's outputs. `align` now has missing inputs and is out of date, but you
   did not ask for its output, so it is not planned. Ask for
   `snakemake -n align` and you get two jobs.

## Exercise 1.3: Spot the error {#ex-1.3}

FastQC does not let you choose its output names. Given
`HCT116_CTCF_1.fastq.gz`, it writes `HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.html` and
`HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.zip`. The rule promises `HCT116_CTCF_1.html` and
`HCT116_CTCF_1.zip`, which nobody writes. Snakemake runs the command, waits a
few seconds for the promised files, and fails the job:

<!-- GENERATE: lesson01-missing-output | stopping-points/stopA | cat > Snakefile <<'EOF'
rule fastqc:
    input:
        "../../data/fastq/HCT116_CTCF_1.fastq.gz",
    output:
        html = "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_1.html",
        zip = "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_1.zip",
    shell:
        "fastqc --outdir output/HCT116_CTCF_1/fastqc {input}"
EOF
snakemake --cores 1 2>&1 | grep -v -e JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS -e '^application/' -e '^Started analysis' -e '^Approx' -e '^Analysis complete' || true -->

{{< generated name="lesson01-missing-output" command="false" >}}

Read the `MissingOutputException` block. It says the job "completed
successfully" (FastQC exited 0), then lists each missing file with what *is*
in its folder: `HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.html, HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.zip`. The
answer is in the error message.

The dry run could not catch this. A dry run checks that the inputs exist or
can be made; it cannot know what a tool will name its files.

The smallest fix is to declare the names FastQC writes:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
    output:
        html = "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.html",   # <1>
        zip = "output/HCT116_CTCF_1/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_1_fastqc.zip",
```

1. Match the tool, not your preferred naming. If you need a different name,
   rename the file in the shell command (`mv`) so the declared output really
   exists when the job ends. Stopping point B does that, because there the
   FASTQ name and the sample name need not agree.

## Exercise 1.4: The default target {#ex-1.4}

One job: `fastqc` for `HCT116_CTCF_1`. With no target on the command line,
Snakemake makes the outputs of whichever rule comes first in the file. The
order of the other rules does not matter at all; Snakemake orders jobs by
their inputs and outputs, not by their place in the file.

That is why every Snakefile in the course, and in the lab's pipelines, starts
with `rule all`: a rule that only lists the final files, so that plain
`snakemake` builds everything. Module 2 writes it.
